messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
Hi folks,

I'm finally getting to grips with GPs, and am now looking at the
multivariate case for application to my real-world data. Specifically,
I deal with EEG data where we get measure voltage as a function of
time and position on the skull. Taking a simple spherical model of the
skull, we can encode position in terms of longitude and latitude (or
phi & theta if you want to use polar coordinates). I see from the
example in the manual how to combine two variables where simple
euclidean distance is computed, i.e. (pg 144):

data {
int<lower=1> D;
int<lower=1> N;
vector[D] x[N];
}
transformed data {
...
Sigma[i,j] <- exp(-dot_self(x[i] - x[j]))
+ if_else(i==j, 0.1, 0.0);
...

Any ideas on how to do this with one simple continuous variate (time)
and spherical coordinates?

Also, if I move to a fitting/inference context where I evaluate the GP
hyperparamters (eta, sigma, rho), presumably something should be done
to reflect the fact that time and spatial coordinates are very
different metrics and therefore might have different best-suited
hyperparameter values, no? The obvious solution would be to have two
additive GPs, one for time and one for the spherical coordinate, and
thus two sets of GP hyperparameters, but I don't want to assume that
the same temporal function exists at all spatial coordinates and vice
versa. Any thoughts?

Thanks in advance,

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
Hi Mike,

I think the answer you are looking for is in the Stan manual, section "Automatic Relevance Detection" (p.147 of the Stan 2.2.0 manual). It basically boils down to allowing rho to vary by dimension. In your case, the two values of rho pertaining to space would be the same, and the third value of rho pertaining to time would be allowed to be estimated separately. Your suggestion of using two additive GPs would mean you would also allow eta to vary between time and space. I'm not sure whether this is necessary; it would add an extra parameter to the model that you might not need.

Best,

Luc

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
As Luc notes the first step would be letting each variable have its own rho.

Spherical coordinates are going to be tricky because they have a different topology
than what Stan can naively handle (S^{n - 1} vs R^{n}).  I’m not sure there’s a great
answer yet — although there had previously been some thoughts on how to make
it work with the addition of some clever priors.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
Oops --- this one got hung up in my drafts.

I think the sphere is the first step to understanding
more general manifold cases. So it'd be natural to do
spheres and then a more general Riemannian manifold case.

Simon Byrne gave a nice talk at MCMski about HMC on a sphere
with geodesics (great circles in the spherical case).

I don't think the spheres are too tricky for either Goodman
and Weare's walker moves or differential evolution updates.

I'm sure Michael could knock out the general definitions
for these ensemble methods if he were so inclined.

For the Goodman and Weare case, the volume adjustment for
Metropolis is going to be tricky (you move along a line there
and need to look at masses of neighborhoods on either end).

For differential evolution, I think you're going to need something
like parallel transport (as seen in Michael's generalization of NUTS)
in order to apply a line of movement between two randomly selected points
to a third point.

- Bob

parts:
Let me try to remember what I did for differential evolution on hypersphere. If you have point A, B and C on surface of hypershere, and want to move from A to A + (B-C):
 
 
- reflect A in B to get A'
- reflect A' in C to get A''
- reflect A'' in A to get A'''
- split A and A'''
 
Simples!
 
Easy enough also to do A + a(B-C)

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
The problem here isn’t geometry (curvature, etc) but rather topology (shape of the manifold).
It’s easy to put together algorithms that will bounce around a hypersphere but it’s much harder
to implement an algorithm that follows the probability mass on the hypersphere. There’s a reason
circular statistics is a notoriously difficult field!

For example, when constructing a trajectory on the hypersphere we have to be careful because
we can’t define a global coordinate system. As Simon has shown you have to be careful when trying
to implement HMC on spaces that aren’t topologically equivalent to R^{n}, such as hyperspheres
and Grassmannian manifolds. There are interesting approaches around, but none would fit

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
On Jun 30, 2014, at 1:12 AM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:

> But maybe DREAM-type MCMC algorithms work on the surface of a hypershere, if you do what I suggest above and do differences by reflection?

Yes, you can do that. Then your moves will be legal and geometrically
sensible if you have a uniform distribution on the surface of a sphere.

But what happens when you have another term in the density? Then you
need to move to a geometry based on the curvature of the log probability.
I think that's what Michael means by saying it's easy to move on the sphere,
but hard to follow the probability mass.

So I think you'd need to generalize the algorithm along the lines of
RHMC to general metrics. I'm not good enough at geometry to do that.
Maybe I should make it a stretch goal (sorry, that pun was intentional).

- Bob

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts:
The original question was on modelling real-valued data on sphere, or actually on sphere and over time. It was not about modelling complex or spherical-valued data. 

So I don't understand what the problem is if one defines a metric on the sphere, something like rho1*arccos(x \dot y) + rho2*(t_x-t_y)^2, a bit like in the beginning of https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/~gentz/pages/WS13/RDS13/slides/A_Lang_RDS13.pdf, and then spans a real-valued gaussian process on that metric. 

What will go wrong? (Except that it will probably be too slow to compute with Stan for realistic EEG data.)

Spatial statistics use the von-Mises-Fisher distribution as an analogue of gaussian on the sphere, and the above (probably, haven't checked) leads to such a kernel for the GP if marginalised over time.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Gaussian Processes on a sphere
parts: Although this is slipping out of the scope of the mailing list, I'd like to add that although a spatiotemporal model for a signal on the sphere is straightforward, I don't see such a simple GP model useful for EEG analysis. (I have done EEG/ERP in the past.) Maybe GP's would make more sense in a more complicated model, though. (Like having a spectral decomposition, or something. The spatial variation is after a convolution, and models that decompose or deconvolve are more useful than smoothing models there.)
